prediction_ref.short_label: Sub-2-bit quantization fits a second 20B-class model under 5 GB by Q2 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary:
PrismML's July 14 release of Bonsai 27B is the origin event for this forecast. The model ships in two extreme-quantization builds: a ternary variant holding weights in {-1, 0, +1} with FP16 scaling at 1.71 effective bits per weight and 5.9 GB, retaining 95% of its full-precision baseline across 15 benchmarks, and a 1-bit binary variant at 1.125 effective bits and 3.9 GB retaining 90%. The second build carries the release — 3.9 GB clears the roughly 6 GB of usable memory an iPhone 17 Pro has left after KV cache and activations, a ceiling that had kept 27B-class weights off handsets outright. The weights are Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face and GitHub, so the encoding is inspectable by anyone attempting to reproduce it.
Two conditions should make the result travel rather than stay a one-off: the artifact is open, and every open-weight family faces the identical memory wall between it and a handset, with whoever clears it first setting which of their models counts as portable. The counterweight is cost — post-training quantization degrades sharply below roughly 3 bits, so holding 90% at 1.125 bits generally implies quantization-aware training or distillation at real expense, which narrows the field to funded labs rather than the hobbyist quantization community. What the day does not supply is the second group: the forecast turns on someone other than PrismML publishing a comparable encoding with its own multi-benchmark retention figure, and today establishes only the first instance.

bridge.narrative: Every number in the driving claim is today's artifact rather than an extrapolation from it: Bonsai 27B's binary build lands at 1.125 effective bits per weight and 3.9 GB, holds 90% of its full-precision baseline across 15 benchmarks, and ships Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face and GitHub. The encoding is public and inspectable, which is what a reproduction attempt needs.

prediction_ref.short_label: x402 settlement counts get an authenticity-filtered public metric by Q2 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary:
The July 14 arXiv preprint by Shengchen Ling, Yajin Zhou, Lei Wu, and Cong Wang is the origin event for this forecast. Because x402 settles AI-agent payments as on-chain stablecoin transactions, its headline adoption metric is a public ledger entry rather than a vendor claim — and it does not survive the audit. Across 280 days of Base chain activity the authors find 136.7 million settlements moving $44.1 million, of which 21.20% are fictitious and 63.78% are internal transfers between wallets in the same linked cluster. The value that demonstrably reaches a named independent service is $187,861.35; the most generous bound, crediting everything not provably manufactured, is $20.2 million, or 45.92%. Payer, recipient, and value Gini coefficients all sit above 0.98, and the manufactured component resolves into a coherent operator-driven economy the authors characterize as star-shaped, machine-timed, and gas-subsidized.
The load-bearing part is their framing: a settlement count measures how cheaply transactions can be manufactured, not how many agents are buying anything. A three-order-of-magnitude gap between the headline and the defensible floor turns an unfiltered count into a liability for whoever publishes it, and agentic commerce is being underwritten by investors and partners on exactly this throughput number — the forcing function the forecast rests on. Absent so far is any response from the measured side: no facilitator, official protocol dashboard, or on-chain analytics provider has published a filtered or net count, nor a documented exclusion methodology.

prediction_ref.short_label: Coding agents ship default-deny sandboxes for untrusted-repo audits by Q2 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary:
Two of today's findings land squarely on this forecast's premise that untrusted-repository review is an execution-layer problem. Mindgard's July 14 disclosure of an unpatched Cursor code-execution flaw makes the point at its sharpest: Cursor searches several filesystem locations for a Git binary when it initializes a project and does not validate executables found in the repository directory itself, so opening a repository carrying a malicious git.exe at its root runs that binary with the user's privileges — no prompt, no approval dialog, no interaction beyond opening the folder — and the lookup repeats on a cadence for as long as the project stays open. Mindgard states the threshold plainly: cloning an untrusted repository merely to read it is enough. The wire-level Grok CLI capture supplies the network half of the same posture, showing that a harness pointed at a repository ships every tracked file's content plus git history to a cloud bucket regardless of what the agent was asked to read.
Both sharpen the reasoning while relocating it. The original driver was that agents cannot separate read code from instructions, so mitigation must move to the execution layer; today's two cases never route through the agent's reading at all — one is the editor's own binary lookup, the other the harness's own upload path — which argues sandboxing and network isolation have to wrap the whole tool rather than only the model's actions. What has not moved is the landing: neither Anthropic nor OpenAI shipped a default-deny audit mode, and the vendor in today's disclosure has not shipped a fix at all.

Cursor searches several filesystem locations for a Git binary when it initializes a project and does not validate executables found in the repo directory itself, so opening a repository carrying a malicious git.exe at its root runs it with the user's privileges, with no prompt and no interaction beyond opening the folder, and the lookup repeats on a cadence while the project stays open.
The mechanism sits outside what the prediction's control would cover, and the disclosure history cuts against its arc. This is an executable lookup rather than an agent file write, so workspace-root confinement and canonical path resolution would not close it. More telling is the vendor side: where the path-traversal and symlink-resolution flaws behind this forecast were assigned CVEs and fixed in Cursor 3.0 — the converge-on-safe-defaults pattern the prediction extrapolates from — today's is unfixed after seven months, with no CVE assigned and no severity score, published on the rationale that continued silence no longer protects anyone.

Today's flaw shares the vendor and the trust assumption while inverting the arc: unfixed after seven months, no CVE, no score, published because silence protects nobody. Confinement and canonical paths would not close a binary lookup anyway.

PrismML's Bonsai 27B, released July 14, extends the exact lineage this forecast is built on: it derives from Qwen3.6 27B — the model whose single-RTX-4090, Apache-2.0, no-MoE package is the prediction's origin evidence — keeps a 262K-token context window, adds multimodal input through a 4-bit vision tower, and ships Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face and GitHub. That an outside lab chose a 27B dense Qwen derivative as the base worth carrying to an entirely new hardware tier is a vote for the recipe's staying power.
The specifics diverge in both directions. The context window is 262K rather than the 1M the prediction pairs with 27B dense, and PrismML is not among the Mistral, Meta, DeepSeek, or Gemma vendors whose convergence the landing requires. More consequentially, Bonsai's argument runs past the prediction rather than toward it: by compressing a 27B-class model to 3.9 GB it moves the memory floor from the RTX 4090's 24 GB down to a handset's budget, which unsettles the hardware anchor the recipe was defined against rather than confirming it.
